division of ''Coleoptera'', including those beetles whose tarsi have normally three joints apiece. Also called ''Pseudotrimera''. See cut under ''lady-bird''. Compare ''Tetramera'' and ''Pentamera'', and see ''tarsal system'' (under ''tarsal''). (''b'') A section of the hymenopterous family ''Chalcididæ'', including the forms with three-jointed tarsi. They all belong to the subfamily ''Trichogramminæ''. See cut under ''Trichogramma''. ''Förster'', 1856.

'''trimeran''' (trim′ẹ-ran), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [< ''trimer-ous'' + ''-an''.] '''I.''' ''a.'' In ''entom.'', same as ''trimerous'', 2.

'''II.''' ''n.'' A trimerous insect; any member of the ''Trimera'', in either sense.

'''trimerite''' (trim′ẹ-rīt), ''n.'' [< Gr. τριμερής, having three parts (see ''trimerous''), + ''-ite''<sup>2</sup>.] A rare mineral consisting of the silicates of beryllium, manganese, and calcium. {{smaller|It occurs in prismatic crystals of hexagonal form, but shown optically to be twins of three triclinic individuals. It is intermediate in form between the manganese silicate (tephroite) and the beryllium silicate (phenacite), and is also related to the latter in form.}}

In ''bot.'', of three members; having the parts or members three in each cycle. Frequently written 3-''merous''.—2. '''trimyarian''' (trim-i-ā′ri-a̤n), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [< Gr. τρεῖς (τρι-), three, + μῦς, a muscle, + ''-arian''.] I. ''a.'' Having three muscular impressions or ciboria on the inner surface of the shell, as a bivalve mollusk: correlated with ''monomyarian'', ''dimyarian'', etc.

'''trinary''' (trī′nạ̄-ri), ''a.'' [< ML. *''trinarius'' (equiv. to L. ''ternarius'': see ''ternary''), < L. ''trini'', three each, threefold: see ''trine.''] Consisting of three parts, or proceeding by threes; ternary.—'''Trinary proposition.''' {{smaller|See ''proposition.''}} '''Trincomali-wood''', ''n.'' See ''halmalille.'' '''trindle''' (trin′dl), ''n.'' [Early mod. E. also ''trindel''; < ME. ''trindel''; a var. of ''trendle'', ''trundle.''] 1. Something round or circular; a ball or hoop; a wheel (especially of a wheelbarrow), or the felly of a wheel. [Obsolete or prov. Eng. or Scotch.] {{smaller block|Ae auld wheelbarrow, mair for token,
Ae leg an' baith the trams are broken;

[< L. ''trimestris'' (see ''trimester'') + ''-al.''] Of or pertaining to a trimester; occurring every three months; quarterly. ''Imp. Dict.'' '''trimetallic''' (trī-me-tal′ik), ''a.'' [< Gr. τρεῖς (τρι-) three, + μέταλλον, metal: see ''metallic.''] Pertaining to or involving the use of three metals, as in currency. [= F. ''trimètre'' = It. ''trimetro'', < L. ''trimetrus'', < Gr. τρίμετρος, containing three measures, < τρεῖς (τρι-), three + μέτρον, measure.] '''I.''' ''a.'' In ''pros.'', consisting of three measures, especially of three iambic measures. '''II.''' ''n.'' In ''pros.'', a verse or period consisting of three measures. {{smaller|A trochaic, iambic, or anapestic trimeter consists of three dipodies (six feet); a trimeter of other rhythms is a hexapody, or period of six feet. The name is specifically given to the iambic trimeter,}} ⏓ – ⏑ – | ⏓ – ⏑ – | ⏓ – ⏑ ⏓, {{smaller|regularly with penthemimeral or hephthemimeral cesur This is the usual verse of the dialogue of the ancient Gre drama.}} ¶ '''trimethylamine''' (trī-meth′il-am-in), ''n.'' [< ''tr'' + ''methyl'' + ''amine''.] A substituted ammoni in which the three hydrogen atoms are r placed by methyl, N(CH3)3. {{smaller|It is prepared fro herring-brine, or more commonly from a waste produ of the beet-sugar manufacture, and is a volatile liqu soluble in water, and having a penetrating fish-like od It has been used in medicine for the treatment of rhe matism.}} '''trimetric''' (trī-met′rik), ''a.'' [< Gr. τρίμετρος, co taining three measures (see ''trimeter''), + ''-ic'' 1. Same as ''trimeter''. ''Amer. Jour. Philol.'', 224.—2. In ''crystal.'', same as ''orthorhombic'', 2. [< ''trim'' + ''-ly''2.] In trim manner; neatly; finely; well. {{smaller block|To ioyne learnyng with cumlie exercises, Conto Bal fœr Castiglione, in his booke, Cortegiane, doth ''trim'' teache. {{right|''Ascham'', The Scholemaster, p.}}}} {{smaller block|This spruce young guest, so ''trimly'' drest. {{right|''Barham'', Ingoldsby Legends, I.}}}} '''trimmer''' (trim′ėr), ''n.'' [< ''trim'' + ''-er''1.] 1. O who or that which trims, in any sense of t word. {{smaller|(''a'') One who arranges or disposes; one who p or keeps in place: as, a grain-''trimmer''.}} {{smaller block|The coal handling plant . . . may be resolved into th parts: The elevators, which discharge the boats, emp ing them of their cargo; the ''trimmers'', which take coal from the elevators and deposit it upon the hea and finally the reloaders. {{right|''Sci. Amer.'', N. S., LXII.}}}} {{smaller|(''b'') One who adjusts as to poise or balance.}} 407 {{smaller block|Who knows but what I might have yielded to the law of nature, that thorough ''trimmer'' of balances? {{right|''R. D. Blackmore'', Lorna Doone, l.}}}} {{smaller|(''c'') One who finishes with trimming; one who decorates or embellishes: as, a coat-''trimmer''; a bonnet-''trimmer''. (''d'') One who cuts, clips, prunes, or pares; specifically, in old use, a barber.}} {{smaller block|At the going out of the halls which belong to the ladies' lodgings were the perfumers and ''trimmers'', through whose hands the gallants past when they were to visit the ladies. {{right|''Urquhart'', tr. of Rabelais, i. 55.}}}} {{smaller|(''e'') A tool used for clipping, pruning, or paring: as, a nail-''trimmer''; a wick-''trimmer''; specifically, a knife or cutting-tool of various forms for trimming the edges of photographs previous to mounting them on cardboard; also, a form of paper-cutter used in bookbinding for trimming the edges of books.}} '''trimorphic''' (trī-môr′fik), ''a.'' [< ''trimorph-ous'' + ''-ic''.] Same as ''trimorphous''. ''Darwin.'' '''trimorphism''' (trī-môr′fizm), ''n.'' [< ''trimorph-ous'' + ''-ism''.] '''1.''' In ''crystal.'', the property of crystallizing in three fundamentally different forms. {{smaller block|Titanium dioxid, TiO2, is an example of trimorphism. In one form it is the mineral octahedrite or anatase; in another, rutile; in a third, brookite.}} '''2.''' In ''biol.'', existence under three distinct forms. It is not rare among insects. {{smaller block|There are, also, cases of dimorphism and ''trimorphism'', both with animals and plants. Thus, Mr. Wallace . . . has shown that the females of certain species of butterflies, in the Malayan archipelago, regularly appear under two or even three conspicuously distinct forms, not connected by intermediate varieties. {{right|''Darwin.''}} Wheel print ''trimmers'', which cut clean edges much better than do knives. {{right|''The Engineer'', LXVII. 298.}}}} [[File:century v08 p0285 c2f1.png|center|93px]] {{c|Trimorphism in Flowers of ''Lythrum Salicaria.''
''a'', the long-styled form; ''b'', the intermediate form; ''c'', the short-styled form; ''s'', style. The calyx and corolla have been removed.}} 2. One who does not openly incline to either side in a contest between parties; hence, one who tries to curry favor with both or with all parties; a time-server. {{smaller|The name was originally given, in English politics, to a party which followed the Marquis of Halifax, during the period from about 1680 to 1690, in trimming between the Whigs and the Tories.}} {{smaller block|The innocent word ''trimmer'' signifies no more than this: That if men are together in a boat, and one part of the company should weigh it down on one side, another would make it lean down as much to the contrary; it happens there is a third opinion, of those who conceive it would do as well if the boat went even without endangering the passengers. {{right|''Marquis of Halifax'', Character of a ''Trimmer'', Pref.}}}} {{smaller block|He who perseveres in error without flinching gets the credit of boldness and consistency, while he who wavers in seeking to do what is right gets stigmatized as a ''trimmer''. {{right|''Irving'', Knickerbocker, p. 270.}}}} 3. In ''bot.'', the occurrence of forms of flowers or other parts upon the same plant, or upon plants of the same species. {{smaller|In trimorphous flowers there are three sets of stamens and pistils, which may be called respectively long-, middle-, and short-length, and in which the pollen from the long stamens is capable of fertilizing only the long-styled forms, the mid-length stamens the mid-styled, etc. Compare ''dimorphism'', and see ''heterogonous trimorphism'', under ''heterogonous''.}} '''trimorphous''' (trī-môr′fus), ''a.''
